AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: To investigate whether self-reported pain during hip strength testing correlates to a large degree with hip muscle strength in soccer players with long-standing unilateral hip and groin pain.

AbstractText.Label: SETTING
AbstractText.content: Clinical assessments at Sports Orthopaedic Research Center-Copenhagen (SORC-C), Arthroscopic Centre Amager, Copenhagen University Hospital, Denmark.

AbstractText.Label: PARTICIPANTS
AbstractText.content: Twenty-four male soccer players with unilateral long-standing hip and groin pain.

AbstractText.Label: INTERVENTIONS
AbstractText.content: The soccer players performed 5 reliable hip muscle strength tests (isometric hip flexion, adduction, abduction, isometric hip flexion-modified Thomas test, and eccentric hip adduction).

AbstractText.Label: MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES
AbstractText.content: Muscle strength was measured with a hand-held dynamometer, and the players rated the pain during testing on a numerical rating scale (0-10).

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: In 4 tests (isometric hip adduction, abduction, flexion, and eccentric adduction), no significant correlations were found between pain during testing and hip muscle strength (Spearman rho = -0.28 to 0.06, P = 0.09-0.39). Isometric hip flexion (modified Thomas test position) showed a moderate negative correlation between pain and hip muscle strength (Spearman rho = -0.44, P = 0.016).

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: Self-reported pain during testing does not seem to correlate with the majority of hip muscle strength tests used in soccer players with long-standing hip and groin pain.

Article.ArticleTitle: Hip Strength Testing of Soccer Players With Long-Standing Hip and Groin Pain: What are the Clinical Implications of Pain During Testing?
